en: The Sutra of the Elder’s Son Bianyi, translated by the Shramana Fachang of the Later Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
Together with twelve hundred and fifty śramaṇas and ten thousand bodhisattvas,
at that time the World-Honored One was seated amidst a vast assembly of countless followers, surrounded by them as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, there was a son of a great elder in the city of Śrāvastī named Bhadramati. Accompanied by five hundred sons of elders, each with their own retinue of five hundred attendants, he came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head to the ground before the Buddha to pay homage, then withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the elder’s son Bianyi, observing that the assembly was seated, received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and rose from his seat. He adjusted his robes, approached with solemn dignity, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to ask a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will graciously explain it.”

World-Honored One, Most True One, you possess the unsurpassed spiritual transformations of the Way and Virtue within the three realms; you deliver all living beings by universally expounding the provisional path, enabling the multitude to find their proper place.

In future ages, the five turbidities will boil over and the three poisons will blaze fiercely; people will burn one another with these conditions, with neither honor nor humility as they harbor poisonous thoughts toward each other. Just as a minister might covet the throne and raise an army to attack his sovereign, only to die and have his name perish.

At that time, calamity shall reach the common people; even among the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples who have received the Buddha’s bequeathed grace and attained the name of "practitioner of the Way," there will be those who outwardly wear the Dharma robes while inwardly harboring jealousy. Lacking reverence and compliance, they shall slander one another, magnify evil and suppress the good, and act with arrogance toward others.

"These people are all destined for the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; they pursue the glory of a single lifetime while remaining ignorant of the calamities of future kalpas. By what means should they be enlightened and transformed?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will fully reveal his teachings, so that future beings may receive this merit, escape the three miserable realms, and dwell forever in halls of bliss.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

Elder’s Son Bianyi, you have let out a lion’s roar before the Buddha, initiating an inspiration that transforms all beings; that those who are ignorant, dark, and wicked in the future may receive this teaching—how truly wonderful it is!
"Regarding what you wish to ask, do not hesitate or find it difficult; the Tathāgata shall explain it to you in detail.
The elder’s son Bianyi addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what causes and conditions does a person attain birth in the heavens?"
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is one born among humans?
By what causes and conditions is one born in the hells?
And by what causes and conditions is one constantly born among the hungry ghosts?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is one born among animals?
By what causes and conditions does one always take birth in a noble family and be honored by the masses?
And by what causes and conditions is one born among slaves and servants, being commanded by others?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is one born among the common people with breath that is fragrant and pure, with body and mind always at peace, praised by others and never slandered?

Again, by what causes and conditions does one obtain birth as a human being who is constantly slandered and loathed by others, whose form is ugly and repulsive, whose body and mind are not at peace, and who always harbors fear?

Furthermore, by what causes and conditions will one, in whatever place one is born, always encounter the Buddhas, hear the Dharma and uphold it without ever deviating from it, meet with spiritual friends and attain a virtuous mind, and if one becomes a śramaṇa, always fulfill one's aspirations?
Such are our questions; we only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain them, so that this assembly may hear the true teaching, and that all beings may attain salvation and peace.
The Buddha said to the elder’s son Bianyi:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well!
I shall explain for you the essential points.
There are five practices by which one may be reborn in the heavens.
What are these five?
First is a mind of loving-kindness: not killing any living beings, nurturing the lives of all creatures, and causing the multitude to attain peace.
Second is being virtuous and upright: not stealing the property of others, practicing generosity without greed, and relieving those who are destitute.
Third, to be chaste and pure, refraining from external lusts, guarding the precepts regarding both men and women, observing the fasts with diligence;
fourth, to be sincere and trustworthy, not deceiving others, guarding against the four faults of speech, and never being covetous or deceitful;
fifth, to abstain from alcohol and not overstep the bounds of verbal conduct.
"By these five things, one attains birth in heaven.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By not killing, one obtains long life; Free from illness, one is always fresh and robust."
All who attain the celestial rank, Their bodies are at ease and radiant light arrives.
By not stealing, they are perpetually great in wealth; Money, treasures, and jewels come to them spontaneously.
The seven precious gems form their palaces, And their hearts always delight in enjoyment.
Neither man nor woman shall engage in sexual misconduct; their bodies will be fragrant, pure, and clean.
Those born [of such conduct] will always be upright in appearance, and their virtuous deeds will naturally be manifest.
Without deceit, their breath will be fragrant, and their speech will always be clear and intelligent.
In discourse one is not stammering; what is spoken is followed by the multitude.
Alcohol and meat do not pass one's mouth; there is no confused or distracted mind.
Wherever one may be born, gods and humans will always attend upon one.
"When their lives come to an end, twenty-five deities will welcome them;
the five blessings will naturally arrive, and their radiance will be most brilliant.
The Buddha said to Bianyi:
"Furthermore, there are five things by which one may be born among human beings.
What are these five?
First, practicing generosity to provide relief and moisture for the poor;..."
Second, maintaining the precepts and not committing the ten evil deeds;
third, practicing patience and not disturbing the minds of others;
fourth, exerting diligence and exhorting those who are indolent.
Fifth, to be single-minded in serving with filial piety and exhausting one's loyalty.
These are the five matters by which one attains birth among humans, becoming wealthy, long-lived, handsome, and majestic, and obtaining the position of a ruler whom all revere and serve.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Through giving, one attains great wealth; Wealth and treasures come naturally.
In whatever birth one is always noble and honored, And immediately inherits the father’s remaining riches."
Always maintaining the precepts in their entirety, Receiving and upholding the teachings of the Triple Gem,
Exerting one's whole heart to refrain from evil, One shall thereby attain a long life.
Practicing patience without disturbing the assembly, And not offending others through anger,
If one does not retaliate when struck or reviled, one will always be handsome in every birth.
If one is diligent and never indolent, constantly mindful of upholding and practicing [the Dharma],
one will always be born powerful and influential, becoming a leader for all.
With single-minded non-retrogression, Loyal faith that never falters,
And serving all elders and superiors— One will encounter no hardships in whatever life one is born.
If one practices these five matters, One shall further become a ruler of men.
"With wealth, power, and handsome appearance, he will naturally become a valiant general.
The Buddha further addressed Bianyi:
"If one commits five types of actions, upon death they shall enter hell and remain there for billions of kalpas before emerging."
What are these five?
First, lacking faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, one slanders and disparages the Noble Path;
second, one destroys Buddhist temples and venerable shrines.
Third, the four classes of followers will slander one another, lacking faith in the retribution of transgressions and devoid of respectful obedience;
fourth, they will become rebellious with no sense of hierarchy, such that rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, will not accord with or follow one another;

fifth, those who wish to practice the Way in the future, once they have attained it, will fail to obey their teachers' instructions, instead becoming arrogant, treating their teachers with contempt, and slandering them.
"These are the five matters by which one dies and enters hell, transmigrating from hell to hell with no time of release.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The foolish people of the world, Do not believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
In my foolish mind, I wish to destroy [the temples], saying that the Buddha possesses no divine power.
Seeing good and evil deeds with my own eyes, I have thus committed various sinful acts;
by destroying the shrines of the gods, I gain little benefit but incur much transgression.
In the final age, those of the fourfold assembly, harboring venom and jealousy,
will slander one another for the sake of fame and profit, unaware that their subsequent retribution will be grave.
Among the various ministers of the world, fathers and sons will treat each other with malice.
For the sake of wealth, treasures, profit, and fame, they harbor no mind of reverence or obedience.
Those evil people of the future who have merely attained the status of śramaṇas will fail to receive and follow their teachers' instructions;
when they die, the retribution they suffer shall not be slight.
"One who commits these five deeds has a transgression that cannot be described;
for billions of kalpas they shall remain in hell, where even the Buddhas cannot save them.
Furthermore, son of a householder!"
There are five types of conduct that lead to rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta). What are these five?
First, stinginess and greed, having no desire to practice giving.
Second, they commit theft and are unfilial toward their two parents;
third, they are ignorant and dark-witted, lacking a heart of compassion;
fourth, they hoard wealth and refuse to provide for their own food and clothing.
"Fifth, failing to provide for one's parents, siblings, wife and children, or servants.
These five matters cause one to fall among the hungry ghosts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Stingy and greedy, they do not practice giving; they pilfer for themselves and fail to support their parents.
Hoarding their wealth, they fear its loss;
they show no compassion toward the elderly, nor do they provide for their wives, children, or servants, withholding everything from them."
Sitting and guarding their wealth until death, the hungry ghosts suffer most grievously.
Their bodies are naked and without clothing; their bellies are vast while their throats are like needles.
They wander east and west seeking food, only to have molten copper poured into their mouths.
Not wishing to drink it, they strike their mouths and force it down;
once a single mouthful enters the belly, the liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach rot away.
Under such arduous suffering, they pass through tens of thousands more years.
Only after their retribution is exhausted do they emerge, being reborn as poor and lowly persons.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
There are another five things by which one performs the conduct of an animal and falls among animals."
What are the five?
First, violating the precepts by secretly committing theft;
second, owing a debt and refusing to repay it.
Third, they repay the taking of life with their own bodies;
fourth, they take no pleasure in hearing or receiving the sutras and the Dharma;
fifth, they constantly rely on worldly conditions and hardships, using fasting, precepts, and assemblies as mere mundane attachments.
"These are the five matters by which one is born among animals.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Constantly stealing people's property in secret, Or owing money and goods while refusing to repay them,"
Delighting in killing, hunting, fishing, and netting; forming worldly attachments and holding unlawful assemblies;
lacking sincerity and faith, and ignorant of the Path—these are matters of the past, the future, and the present.
Committing various sins without self-awareness, one gradually accumulates karma and falls among the animals—oxen, horses, elephants, donkeys, and camels; pigs, sheep, and dogs beyond counting.
Constantly burdened by heavy loads and dying to have their skins flayed, such suffering is truly unbearable.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
There are five other matters by which one becomes noble and is respected by the multitude.
What are these five?
First, practicing generosity extensively and universally;
second, paying homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and all elders;
third, practicing patience without harboring anger or resentment.
Fourth, being gentle, harmonious, humble, and deferential;
fifth, being extensively learned and reciting the sutras and precepts.
These five matters enable one to attain nobility and be revered by all people.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"With a mind always equal in giving, Universally rescuing all to bring peace to the multitude;
Physical beauty, strength, longevity, and freedom from illness— All kin and friends receive this grace."
Those who revere the Triple Gem and serve their elders and superiors will be born into noble and honorable circumstances and shall always receive the respect of all.
Those who practice patience and are free from anger will invariably be born with handsome features.
All people see him with joy; gazing upon him, they never tire.
His mind is disciplined and gentle; he is humble, yielding, and respectful.
Studying and reciting the sutras, he is thus the most honored among men.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
There are five things that cause one to be constantly born into lowly and base circumstances as a servant or slave.
What are these five?
First, being arrogant and disrespectful toward one's parents;
second, being stubborn and lacking a mind of reverence;
third, being heedless and failing to pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Fourth, making theft one's livelihood;
fifth, incurring debt and fleeing without repaying it.
These five matters cause one to be constantly born among lowly and base slaves.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there be a foolish person Who is arrogant toward his parents,
Lacking a heart of reverence and respect, He shall subsequently be born into a lowly and base station."
Failing to pay homage to or serve the Triple Gem, being stubborn and disrespectful toward elders,
and lacking compassion or filial piety toward others, one will be born as a slave upon birth.
Indulging one's own mind and will, one steals the wealth and property of others.
Refusing to repay one's debts leads to rebirth among slaves;
dependent on others for food and clothing, one is driven as a servant without autonomy.
One must labor to repay the master until the karmic debt is exhausted, at which point one may finally escape.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!

There are five more things by which one is born among humans, with breath that is fragrant and pure, body and mind always at peace, praised by others and not subjected to slander. What are these five? First, one does not harbor anger toward sentient beings; second, one does not harbor malice toward sentient beings; third, one does not harbor resentment toward sentient beings; fourth, one does not harbor hatred toward sentient beings; fifth, one does not harbor ill will toward sentient beings. Son of a householder, if one possesses these five qualities, one will be born among humans with breath that is fragrant and pure, body and mind always at peace, praised by others and not subjected to slander."
What are these five?
First, to be sincere and not deceive others;
second, to recite the sutras without making distinctions between "this" and "that."
Third, to guard one's speech and refrain from slandering the Noble Path;
fourth, to teach others to distance themselves from evil and draw near to goodness;
fifth, not to seek out the faults or shortcomings of others.
"These are the five matters by which one is born among humans with fragrant and pure breath, constant peace of body and mind, and praise from others rather than slander.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Revering the Triple Gem, Not being arrogant toward one's parents,"
Utmost sincerity and freedom from deception are what those who practice the Way revere.
Guarding one’s speech so as not to slander, maintaining an impartial mind toward all beings,
encouraging others to distance themselves from unwholesome deeds, and reciting, studying, and contemplating the True Dharma.
When people in the world are free from arrogance, Respecting one another as they would their own parents,
Restraining evil and promoting the good— In this way, one attains Buddhahood swiftly.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!

Furthermore, there are five matters by which one who is among human beings will constantly be slandered, loathed by others, possess an ugly physical form, have an unsettled mind, and always harbor fear.
What are these five?
First, they are constantly lacking sincerity and deceive others;
second, when there is a great assembly where the Dharma is being preached, they slander it.
Third, seeing fellow students, they treat them with contempt and test them;
fourth, not seeing any fault in others, they fabricate transgressions against them;
fifth, they engage in double-tongued speech to sow discord between parties.

These are the five matters by which one, if born among humans, will constantly suffer slander, be detested by others, have an ugly physical form, and experience mental unrest while always harboring fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Deceiving and deluding the multitude, Always lacking sincerity,
Acting with discordance between mind and speech— This causes the body to receive heavy retribution."
If one is born within the hells, an iron hook will pull out one’s tongue,
and molten copper will be poured into one’s mouth, day and night without ceasing.
If one should be born as a human, the breath will always be foul and putrid.
People see them and are displeased; there is no harmony, joy, or gladness.
They constantly encounter matters involving government officials and are subjected to the ridicule and criticism of others.
Meeting with manifold calamities and hardships, their minds are from the outset unsettled.
Upon death they return to hell; when released, they become animals.
Wandering through the five realms of existence, they do not escape manifold sufferings and hardships.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!

Furthermore, there are five matters: wherever one is born, one will always be in the company of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, never being separated from them; upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one immediately attains a virtuous mind; and if one becomes a śramaṇa, one shall attain one's aspirations.
What are the five?
First, to personally honor the Three Jewels and exhort others to do so;
second, to create images of the Buddha and ensure they are kept fresh and clean.
Third, they constantly follow their teacher’s instructions and do not violate what they have received;
fourth, they extend universal compassion to all beings, regarding them as equal to themselves, just as one loves an only child;
fifth, they recite the sutras and teachings they have received day and night.

These are the five matters: wherever one is born, one will always be in the company of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, never being separated from them; upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one immediately gains a virtuous mind; and if one becomes a śramaṇa, one shall attain one's aspirations.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Reverently honor the Triple Gem; teach and exhort others to serve it.
Fashion beautiful images of the Buddha, and uphold the instructions of all venerable teachers."
One should regard all people as no different from oneself;
when self and others are entirely equal, one practices this and meets before the Buddha.
Constantly studying day and night, wisdom is the great treasure.
"Awakening all who are blind and in darkness, you cause them all to universally know the truth of the Way.

Thereupon, the elder’s son Bianyi, having heard the Buddha explain the meaning of these fifty essential dharmas, was filled with joy and attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). All five hundred sons of elders likewise attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra*), and each member of the assembly realized their own aspirations.
Thereupon, Bianyi rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!
Please expound this Dharma so that those gathered here may hear its essence, and furthermore, so that future beings may be delivered from their hardships.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will pass through our poor village and its assembly, and deign to accept a meal at our home tomorrow at noon.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
The sons of the elders prostrated themselves before the Buddha and departed with joy.
Bianyi returned home and said to his parents:
“The one we have now invited is rare among men; his name is the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Dharma Master, peerless throughout the three realms.
He then informed his wife, instructing her to prepare a meal, which she immediately prepared in full.
The next day, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, went to his house and sat with solemn dignity.
At that time, the elder’s son Bianyi, along with his parents and kinsmen, came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and each attended to him with offerings.
Bianyi rose and performed the ritual washing of water, then respectfully presented the food.

Before the meal was finished, a beggar came forward and walked past the seats begging for alms; as the Buddha had not yet offered his blessing, no one dared to give anything. Having gone through the entire assembly without obtaining anything, the beggar departed in a fit of rage and gave rise to an evil thought:
"These śramaṇas are indolent, foolish, and deluded; what kind of Way do they possess?"
When a poor person begged from him, he had no intention of giving.
The elder was deluded, thinking, "I am feeding these people with no heart of compassion.
"If I were a king," he thought, "I would crush his head with an iron-rimmed chariot!"
Having spoken thus, he departed.

After the Buddha had finished giving his blessing (*dakṣiṇā*), a beggar came in to beg for alms. Everyone in the assembly gave him something; having received a great amount of food, he left with joy and immediately thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas all possess a compassionate heart; pitying my poverty and cold, they have given me food until I am full, which will sustain me for several days."
"Excellent!
That you, O Householder, are able to serve such great beings brings immeasurable merit.
As a king, I shall provide offerings to the Buddha and his disciples; for seven days, I shall repay the kindness of your relief from hunger and thirst today."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
After the Buddha had finished eating and preached the Dharma, he returned to the vihāra.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"From this day forward, after the alms have been distributed, you shall eat your food; let this be your constant practice.
At that time, the two beggars wandered from place to place begging for alms until they reached another kingdom, where they lay down amidst the thick grass by the roadside.
At that time, the king suddenly passed away, leaving no heir.
The royal astrologer, who was well-versed in the science of physiognomy, recorded in his prophetic chronicles:
"A person of humble origin shall become the king."
The ministers, officials, and their retinue of thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen traveled throughout the kingdom to determine who should be king.
Looking about, they saw above a patch of deep grass by the roadside a canopy of clouds.
The physiognomist pointed and said:
"Among these is a divine man!
He then saw the beggar, who was the one destined to be king.
The various ministers prostrated themselves in audience, each addressing him as "Your Majesty.
The beggar was struck with astonishment; he declared himself to be low-born and not of royal lineage.
They all said, "He possesses the auspicious marks; it is not by force that he has attained this."

Having bathed in fragrant water and donned the robes of a king, his radiant marks were solemn and majestic; praised boundlessly, he led the way with attendants before and behind as he turned his carriage to enter the kingdom.
At that time, the man of evil intent was lying asleep in deep grass and did not wake; the chariot rolled over him and severed his head.
When the king arrived in the kingdom, the yin and yang were harmonized, the four seasons flourished with brilliance, and the people lived in peace and happiness, extolling the virtue of the king.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"By what causes and conditions did this man, who was once poor, become a king?
Formerly, when he was begging for alms, he received the Buddha's grace and obtained a great amount of food; thereupon, a wholesome thought arose within him:"
"Having attained the status of a king, I have been able to make offerings for seven days;
the Buddha’s grace and virtue have now borne fruit.
He immediately summoned his ministers and, facing the kingdom of Śrāvastī from afar, burned incense and paid homage.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha, saying:
"Having received the World-Honored One’s grace, I have become a king of men.
I pray that you will deign to bend your divine majesty and come to transform the ignorant and deluded people of this land, so that they may receive your instruction."
Thereupon, the Buddha told his disciples,
"You should accept their invitation.
The Buddha, together with a multitude of his disciples numbering in the infinite, proceeded to that country.
At that time, the king went out to welcome him; together with his various ministers, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, burned incense, scattered flowers, and made offerings of music.
Once the Buddha had entered the palace, he took his seat; the king rose to offer water for washing and prepared a meal, which was completed in a short while.
At that time, the king prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"I was originally a lowly person; by what meritorious conduct have I come to enjoy this position?"
"I pray that the Buddha will explain this, so that the people of this land may receive the opening of their eyes.
The Buddha told the king:
"In the past, there was a son of an elder in the city of Śrāvastī named Bianyi (Vaiśravaṇa), who prepared a great offering and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha."

At that time, the Buddha was seated and had finished his meal but had not yet given the blessing of thanks. A beggar came in wishing to solicit alms, but having received nothing at all, he departed in a fit of rage. An evil thought arose within him, and he said:
"If I become king, I shall crush the heads of these monks with an iron-rimmed chariot!"
Later, another person arrived who obtained a great deal of food through begging; upon leaving, he thought to himself:
"If I were to become king, I would provide offerings to this assembly of noble monks for seven days."
The one who was "Good Thought" at that time is the present King;

the one who was "Evil Thought," lying in the deep grass, was run over and his head severed by the chariot, cavalry, and attendants as the King accepted his rightful position and turned his carriage back into the kingdom. Having died, he entered hell, where he was crushed by a flaming chariot, remaining there for a hundred million kalpas before finally emerging.
"The King has now invited the Buddha; his fulfillment of his vow is exceedingly generous. He shall receive blessings in every lifetime without end.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The human mind is the root of poison, The mouth is the gate of calamity."
What one intends in the mind and speaks with the mouth, the body receives as its retribution and calamity.
One who does not distinguish between good and evil people brings suffering upon themselves by their own actions;
though they intended only to harm another, they did not realize the wheel had crushed their own head.
The mind is the nectar-like Dharma, which causes one to be born in the heavens;
what the mind intends and the mouth speaks, the body receives as its merit.
Those who contemplate both good and evil within themselves create the very foundation for their own well-being.
"Direct all thoughts toward what is wholesome, Like a king who has attained his royal throne.
At that time, the king heard the sutra and rejoiced; the ministers and citizens throughout the entire kingdom attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

After making offerings to the Buddha for seven days, the Buddha wished to depart. The king, his ministers, and the common people paid homage to the Buddha and took their leave; thereupon, the World-Honored One returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
The venerable Ānanda adjusted his robes, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what name should this sutra be known, and how should it be practiced?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Questions of the Elder’s Son Bianyi'; you should uphold it. It is also known as 'The Essential Meaning of All Dharmas'."
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:

"If there are good men or good women who practice this sutra, uphold it, recite it, proclaim it to future generations, and cause others to receive and uphold it, the merit of such persons will be no different from that of serving my own person."
"Those who recite this sutra shall receive the prediction of enlightenment from Maitreya Buddha; what the Tathāgata speaks with his broad and long tongue is without deviation.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the devas, nāgas, spirits, and the fourfold assembly of disciples, having heard the sutra, rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Bianyi (Vimalakīrti)
